stations.title: Where your power comes from
caption: Sun, wind and batteries make it.
An inverter is the gate it all passes through.

stations.title: The old heartbeat
caption: Big spinning generators set the rhythm: 60 Hz.
Their sheer weight keeps it steady when demand jumps.

number.source: Nominal grid frequency in North America

stations.title: Losing the heartbeat
caption: Solar, wind and batteries have no spinning mass.
As the old plants retire, that steadying weight goes with them,
and the same bump shakes the frequency harder.
stations.hint: Try it: drag left or right to change the inertia

stations.title: Follow or lead
caption: Most inverters only follow. They copy the grid's voltage, so when the grid drops, they shut off.
A grid-forming inverter makes its own voltage and frequency, so the lights stay on.

stations.title: Why the grid needs them
caption: A grid full of followers needs something to follow.
Grid-forming inverters can be that something. They hold up islands, restart a grid after a blackout,
and keep weak lines steady with no spinning machine at all.

stations.title: Inside the box
caption: This one is my design. It does the same job as a grid-scale unit, scaled down to about 1 kW.
It starts with 400 V of DC, held stiff by two capacitors.

number.source: DC source 400 V; DC-link 2 × 220 µF, 450 V. Manual V11 and V12

stations.title: Six fast switches
caption: One module chops the DC into pulses,
10,000 times a second.

number.source: Infineon IKCM20L60GD IGBT module, 600 V / 20 A, switched at 10 kHz. Manual V11

stations.title: Pulses in, sine out
caption: Coils smooth the current. Capacitors smooth the voltage.
What leaves is a clean 60 Hz wave.

number.source: LC filter 2 mH + 20 µF per phase, resonance about 800 Hz. Manual V13, D21

stations.tierNote: Coil and capacitor shapes: representative parts

stations.title: A flywheel made of math
caption: The controller measures power and spins a virtual flywheel.
It is the old heartbeat, rebuilt in software.
stations.source: Virtual synchronous machine, manual V7; final values V13
stations.tierNote: Controller board: typical part, not specified in this design

stations.title: Lean, don't break
caption: More load? The frequency eases down a little and holds.
Doubling the load cost about 0.3 Hz.

number.source: Load step from 8.4 Ω to 4.2 Ω: 59.857 Hz to 59.554 Hz. V13, D26

stations.title: Holding the voltage
caption: A fast loop compares the wave it wants with the wave it has.
They agree to within 0.12 %.

number.source: Capacitor voltage error at base load: −0.12 % (inverter 1), −0.04 % (inverter 2). V13, D14

stations.tierNote: Voltage sensor: typical part, not specified in this design

stations.title: Ten amps, no more
caption: A short circuit hits the output.
The current is held at 10 A instead of running away.

number.source: Bolted fault on the shared bus: 9.999 A and 10.001 A, limit 10 A. V13, D27

stations.tierNote: Current sensors: typical parts, not specified in this design

stations.title: Keeping it cool
caption: A finned heatsink and a fan carry the heat away.
The hottest point stays under its 125 °C limit.

number.source: IGBT junction 110.6 °C at heavy load, 119.2 °C with a fan failure; design limit 125 °C. Heatsink 0.47 K/W under the module (FEA). D1, manual V11

stations.title: Sharing without talking
caption: Two of my units feed one bus. A load step hits,
and one picks up exactly twice the other's share. 2:1, automatically.
stations.hint: Try it: drag up or down to change the load

stations.title: Many leaders, one grid
caption: On a real grid the units are far bigger, but the rule is the same.
A disturbance arrives, and they all lean in and absorb it together.
stations.source: Theory note 03; the same droop law as station 14

stations.title: Thirteen versions later
caption: I built this in 13 versions, all in simulation: a small-scale version of what a grid-forming plant does.
The details, the mistakes and the sources are one click away.
